biggestGap: The chessmen have silhouettes now but no SKIN: the pale army is uniform clean cold white with none of the film's irregular rust-ochre blotching, and every helm, torso, cape and shield is a smooth unbroken surface with zero carved incident (brow ridges, mail rings, shield rims and bosses, tabard/drapery folds, tooled chisel texture) — so mid-band detail sits at 0.0061 against the film's 0.0222, and each piece reads as an unfinished clay maquette rather than carved, stained limestone.
critiqueDetail:
This is a real advance on round 1 and it deserves to be said plainly: the featureless tapered cones are gone. The plinths are now genuinely good — brightened crops of the mid-right plinths show true hexagonal stepped stone with a legible profile stack (plinth block, cavetto, torus, a dentil/colonnette course under the cap), read as architecture and not as discs. Limb geometry exists: separated legs, hunched pawn shells, cape masses, an occasional blade. The round-1 headline gap is closed.

But the blind pair was still instant and total. Panel B carried carved combatants with legible helms, mail, shields and mottled orange-brown limestone; panel A was mine. The failure has inverted since round 1: then detailTotal was ABOVE the film (0.0233 vs 0.0135) because faceting noise stood in for carving. Now it is far BELOW — 0.00552 vs 0.01807, a 3.3x deficit, and the band shape is deficient at every scale rather than misallocated: fine 0.00402 vs 0.00872 (0.46x), mid 0.00605 vs 0.02218 (0.27x), coarse 0.00655 vs 0.02350 (0.28x). The rebuild bought silhouette and moulding but spent nothing on surface. Zoomed and brightened, the near pawn shells are smooth ovoid masses with no helmet brow, no pauldron, no shield boss, no rivets; the dark king's cape is a single glassy sheet with no mail grain; the pale stone shows no staining anywhere in frame. gradientAnisotropy 1.116 vs 1.982 confirms it — the film's edge energy is strongly oriented (courses, mouldings, mail rows, drapery ribs all running in families); ours is nearly isotropic, i.e. noise and blur, not carving.

Second, the palette is still inverted and is now worse than round 1 on warmth balance: meanLitHueDeg 14.1 vs reference 212 (delta -197.9), warmFraction 0.1668 vs 0.0031, coolFraction 0.1949 vs 0.5181, meanSaturation 0.3263 vs 0.2924. A single blown flame at frame left (fracBlown 0.0201 vs the reference's 0.0000) is dumping orange light across the entire pale army, so the one place the brief allows warmth — rust and ochre staining as pigment in the stone — is instead being faked by an orange key. That is exactly backwards: the film's limestone is warm in ALBEDO and cold in LIGHT.

Third, framing is destroying what figuration does exist. The camera sits below plinth-cap height and the near pieces are cropped headless at the top of frame, so the shot's stated subject — a mounted knight with a cross-slit conical helm, chainmail cape and curved blade — is not in the image at all. Combined with a defocus that reaches the near-camera subject (the brief demands background defocused, SUBJECT SHARP), fracShadow 0.7055 vs 0.5372 and histogramEntropy 5.842 vs 6.861, most of the frame is unreadable black. I am judging pieces, not camera, so this is not my headline — but the piece team should know that even a perfectly carved knight would be invisible in this setup.

history.gap: The pieces have no figurative geometry at all — every foreground chessman is a featureless tapered low-poly cone with visible flat-shaded facets, where the film frame shows armoured riders on rearing horses with cross-slit conical helms and curved sabres, crouching domed-helm pawns, and a huge draped chainmail cape, each on a hexagonal stepped moulded plinth.
